The results suggest that multi-layer defenses, reinforced by built-in behavioral constraints, substantially limit what prompt engineering alone can achieve.

title: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reasoning Systems for Knowledge-Grounded Material Substitution
abstract: AI-assisted scientific discovery increasingly seeks to move beyond generating plausible ideas toward reproducible, constraint-aware workflows that can support practical engineering decisions. We present MARS, a hierarchical Multi-Agent Reasoning System for knowledge-grounded material substitution under scientific and manufacturing constraints. We apply MARS to replace per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), a demanding materials-design problem in which substitutes must satisfy functional performance, environmental, experimental, and processing requirements. MARS decomposes substitution into a closed-loop workflow comprising requirement analysis, grounded candidate generation, and manufacturability assessment with process design. The system integrates retrieval-augmented generation, knowledge-graph reasoning, a database of lab-available materials, persistent memory of intermediate results, and rejection-aware iterative feedback. In a PFAS-substitution case study, MARS generates structured material requirements, identifies an evidence-grounded substitute candidate, and develops a lab-scale manufacturing route. In a multi-seed ablation evaluation, MARS achieves the highest overall performance across all three subsystems, with gains that persist when the backbone model is held fixed. These results suggest that hierarchical decomposition, knowledge grounding, and manufacturability-aware refinement improve material-substitution reasoning beyond model capability alone.

title: Conserved amount, negotiable placement. Prompting perturbs one architecture, an AI reviewer both
abstract: Tesler's conservation law holds that a problem carries an irreducible amount of complexity. Brooks separates that essential part from the accidental part a solution adds. If the essential part is fixed, architecture is placement rather than quantity, and the question is which levers move placement. An AI agent implements sixty accumulating change requests on one REST endpoint under two architectures, a mutative Spring controller and an additive OfficeFloor pipeline, under five conditions, ten runs per cell, model fixed. Four are external controls, from a bare change request to the disclosed structural cost function. The fifth is different in kind. A second agent reviews each change and reasons about cohesion itself. Amount is steady. Across all ten cells the finished complexity varies by 7% to 20% over four operationalisations, and the complexity the sixty rules added by 21% to 29% within an architecture. Placement is not. Under the four external controls the plasticity ratio between the architectures is near 1 on six amount metrics (five of six intervals contain 1) against 2.7 to 10.0 on eleven placement metrics (ten of eleven above 1). The mutative architecture moves, the additive one does not, and the disclosed formula brings it to the additive arm's untouched placement. The AI reviewer is the one lever that moves the additive arm, on one family only. It consolidates the pipeline, raising change- and mass-concentration on every such metric, interval excluding zero, while leaving coupling, file count and per-node complexity untouched. The price is reported in full. Strict correctness fell in most comparisons though each rule was implemented correctly in over 99% of checkpoints, and all three outcome measures favour the concentrated codebase. The contribution is a measurable property of an architecture and its lever, not a verdict on either.

title: Branching fraction measurement of the $B^0\to K^+π^-μ^+μ^-$ decay at high dihadron mass
abstract: This Letter presents the first measurement of the $B^{0} \to K^{+}π^{-}μ^{+}μ^{-}$ differential branching fraction in the region of the dihadron $K^+π^-$ mass, $m_{Kπ}$, $1000< m_{Kπ} < 1835\,\text{MeV}/c^{2}$. This decay mode is mediated by the quark-level transition $b \to s\ell^{+}\ell^{-}$, for which the measured effective couplings show tensions with Standard Model predictions. The analysis is performed using proton-proton collision data collected with the LHCb detector between 2011 and 2018, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of $8.4\,\text{fb}^{-1}$. The differential branching fraction is determined across different regions of dimuon mass squared, $q^2$, in the interval $0.1 < q^2 < 18.0\,\text{GeV}^2/c^{4}$, as well as in different regions of $ m_{Kπ}$ in the interval $1.1 < q^2 < 6.0\,\text{GeV}^2/c^{4}$. The results represent the first differential measurement of the branching fraction across $m_{Kπ}$ within the selected dihadron-mass region, and the first observation of the decay within this region above the $J/ψ$ resonance.

authors.name: U. De Freitas Carneiro Da Graca

title: A Pipeline for the AI-Assisted Analysis of Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer Observations of Black Hole X-ray Binaries and Limits on Their Polarization Variability
abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) has opened a new window into the high-energy Universe, with the capability to measure the arrival time, arrival direction, energy, and, for the first time with the required sensitivity, the polarization of X-rays from black holes, neutron stars, and other cosmic sources of X-rays. In this paper, we discuss the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents for the analysis of IXPE data. The pipeline combines an immutable code base with evolving knowledge databases. The generation of analysis projects makes use of a literature data base to judge the novelty of the proposed analysis projects. We emphasize that the analysis requires two types of expert knowledge: detailed instructions about how to reduce the X-ray data, and expert knowledge about how to interpret the results. We employ several levels of auditors that scrutinize the analysis plan, the analysis scripts, and the analysis results for data and method adequacy. The pipeline includes a staggered approach to interpret the analysis results. We present exemplary results from the pipeline applied to IXPE observations of Black Hole X-ray Binaries (BHXRBs) including comparisons of results from the analysis pipeline with published results and a systematic search for polarization degree and polarization angle variability in long IXPE observations. We critically discuss the performance of the pipeline and future avenues for improving it.

title: Observation-Referenced Tissue Deformation Forecasting with Tool-Driven and Residual Dynamics
abstract: Forecasting tissue deformation from future instrument motion could support predictive planning and increasingly autonomous surgical systems. We study this problem using a scene-specific differentiable surface model fitted to an observed tool-tissue interaction window. Rather than forecasting absolute simulated positions, we introduce an \textit{observation-referenced} formulation that anchors each tissue point to its last valid observation and adds only the deformation induced by the known, preplanned future tool trajectory. This reduces sensitivity to reconstruction, initialization, and persistent simulation offsets while preserving the predicted deformation response. The physical model uses differentiable, mesh-free position-based dynamics with scene-specific rigidity, attachment, region scale, and grasp coupling. We further introduce an optional \textit{observation-referenced residual model} combining graph-spectral spatial modes with periodic harmonic dynamics for structured motion not explained by the tool input. We evaluate the framework retrospectively on 12 surgical manipulation clips from three datasets. Observation referencing provides the largest gain, with a median within-clip error ratio of $0.598$ relative to the corresponding absolute simulation forecast. The optional periodic residual further improves forecasting when the remaining motion exhibits periodic structure. These results support observation-referenced deformation prediction as a practical building block for future surgical world models, digital twins, and generative simulators that must predict how tissue evolves under instrument actions.

title: Agentic Data Engineering for LLMs: System Design and a Controlled Empirical Study
abstract: LLM data engineering requires iterative experimentation to determine how data selection, rewards, and curricula affect model learning, making it a natural setting for AI-for-AI (AI4AI) research. Can agents use experimental feedback to progressively improve strategies, and do the resulting strategies improve target-model performance on held-out data? We study how agents use experimental feedback to develop data-engineering strategies under fixed training and evaluation protocols. Our Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework lets agents pursue, revise, or combine research directions using cumulative findings. Strategies are selected by in-loop scores and evaluated on held-out benchmarks. Across four tasks-math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning-selected strategies achieve absolute gains over generic baselines of up to 13.34% on AIME25 Pass@32 and 5.85% averaged across four held-out benchmarks under fixed training conditions. In-loop scores improve over successive experiments, while held-out trajectories show that later in-loop gains do not always improve generalization. Comparisons of research organization and feedback access favor combining evidence analysis with cumulative findings. Research trajectories show how earlier findings inform strategy revisions and combinations across research directions.

title: Learning Non-Gaussian SEMs with Conditional Risk, and Why the Direction of Recursion Matters
abstract: Variance-based methods recover a Gaussian linear structural equation model (SEM) with equal or suitably constrained error variances, either by recursively identifying the source nodes with smallest conditional variance (top-down method) or sink nodes with highest conditional variance (bottom-up method). We show that the use of conditional variance is incidental: replacing it with the conditional risk, i.e., the minimal expected loss of linear prediction under the negative log-likelihood of the noise distribution, extends both methods to non-Gaussian noise. Existing methods are the least-squares special case. This yields two main results. First, exploiting the noise distribution improves structure recovery: the matched-loss procedures recover the SEM more accurately than their least-squares counterparts and the LiNGAM methods, which are designed for non-Gaussianity. Second, the two methods, interchangeable in the Gaussian setting, separate under non-Gaussian noise: the top-down method is correct for every noise density with finite differential entropy, whereas the bottom-up method requires a regularity condition and can fail without it, for instance under mean-zero exponential or Cauchy noise. Simulations confirm both results.

title: Real-Time Traffic Density Estimation: A Hybrid Computer Vision and Predictive Machine Learning Pipeline
abstract: Traffic density estimation from camera feeds requires connecting visual perception with short-horizon forecasting. We present a two-stage pipeline that combines vehicle detection and tracking with a spatial logic layer, followed by a temporal estimator. The spatial layer filters bounding boxes by their overlap with a precomputed road mask and extracts per-frame traffic features. LSTM, GRU, and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) estimators use these features to predict five future steps from a ten-frame input window. We benchmark ten detector variants from six families on a dataset of 5,716 annotated frames using a single NVIDIA GPU. YOLOv5l achieves the highest mAP@50:95 of 0.524 at 56 frames per second, while YOLOv8n reaches 258 frames per second at 0.487 mAP@50:95; these rates measure detector inference without tracking or spatial filtering. Temporal evaluation on 29,243 held-out windows yields aggregate R-squared values of 0.858 for GRU, 0.856 for LSTM, and 0.840 for TCN. These metrics measure forecasts of detector-derived telemetry and are dominated by direction variance, rather than establishing absolute traffic-density accuracy. No road mask was available for the evaluation stream, limiting validation of the spatial filtering component. A live run on a third camera stream examines forecasting behavior within the complete pipeline. The results characterize detector speed-accuracy trade-offs and the limitations of short-window traffic telemetry forecasting.

title: Continuous-Time Cloth Dynamics with Physics-Informed Neural ODEs
abstract: We present ContinuousCloth, a continuous-time, physics-informed neural solver for deformable cloth dynamics that enforces a spring--mass ODE within a neural trajectory model. Unlike classical time-stepping simulators that return trajectories only on a discrete integration grid, ContinuousCloth supports querying at arbitrary timestamps and computing displacement, velocity, and acceleration via automatic differentiation. We evaluate ContinuousCloth along two dimensions. In a physics-only setting, ContinuousCloth achieves trajectory accuracy comparable to high-precision solvers across six diverse boundary-condition scenarios while reducing runtime by up to 17.4 times. When fused with sparse and noisy observations, the spring--mass ODE acts as a strong inductive bias for downstream tasks: interpolation and parameter estimation. That is, ContinuousCloth reduces interpolation error by 7.3 times over a data-only neural baseline in simulation and 2.4 times on real-world cloth sequences, and achieves 2.6 times lower parameter error than a differentiable-solver baseline under high-noise conditions, demonstrating consistent robustness under realistic measurement imperfections.

title: Natural Code Transformation Confuses Agents in Vulnerability Analysis
abstract: Having demonstrated a strong potential for automating vulnerability discovery, AI agents can also be used to attack software systems at scale. Today's software systems need mechanisms to level the playing field by slowing down potential attacks, giving them time to patch vulnerabilities and strengthen software. Along this line, our study of agent trajectories in vulnerability analysis shows a surprising finding: agents produce dramatically different results across real-world code commits that carry the same functionality and the same vulnerability. This phenomenon appears consistently in multiple code domains and vulnerability categories. It motivates us to study natural and functionality-preserving code transformations derived from real-world software development, and their potential as a defense against attacker agents. We build a corpus of natural transformations by mining recurring development patterns from real-world code commits, and apply them to evaluate impact on agentic vulnerability analysis. Our results show that even a single form of transformation can effectively "confuse" frontier agents, e.g., Codex with GPT-6 Sol, reducing successes in vulnerability discovery. We also study different agent failures, whether transformations can be composed to provide stronger protection, and adaptive attackers who seek to reverse them. Overall, our study of natural code transformation significantly expands the research space of using code transformations to defend against malicious agents.

title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while keeping the environment coherent across repeated observations and interventions and preserving objective ground truth. We introduce ACED-BENCH (Active Causal Evidence and Decision Benchmark), a neuro-symbolic benchmark built around this requirement. The key idea is to separate the readable scientific surface from the formal causal world: LLMs generate natural-language scenarios and task text, while hidden probabilistic graphical models define the causal graph, data-generating process, intervention semantics, validation checks, and oracle answers. This yields scientific worlds that are natural for agents to investigate but exact enough for scalable, programmatic evaluation. The main leaderboard ACED-CORE contains 180 tasks: 60 set-valued causal ancestry/descendancy questions and 120 constrained causal-decision tasks. We also report ACED-QUAL, a 150-question yes/no qualification check using the same hidden-PGM interface. We evaluate seven contemporary LLMs and two earlier-generation models across three active agent designs. ACED-QUAL checks whether agents can use the interface to draw conclusions from evidence, while ACED-CORE tests whether they can decide what evidence to collect and when to commit to an answer. Evidence-ledger analysis localizes failures within the investigation: agents test the wrong intervention, lose relevant evidence, or continue after sufficient evidence has appeared. These results suggest that reliable AI co-scientists need explicit support for experiment design, evidence retention, answer commitment, and stopping.

title: ANASSA: From High-Level Framework to Low-Level Architecture for Spatial Agentic AI
abstract: Agentic AI systems operating over geospatial data require more than autonomous reasoning and tool use; they must also support explicit orchestration, spatial validation, governance, provenance, failure handling, and human decision authority. Prior work introduced ANASSA, an agentic AI orchestration framework for spatial intelligence that established high-level components and responsibility boundaries for governed agentic execution (arXiv:2609.14824). However, the framework did not specify how those high-level responsibilities should be systematically decomposed into an implementation-facing low-level architecture. This paper addresses that gap by applying Design Science Research (DSR) to refine the ANASSA framework from high-level architectural (HLA) responsibilities into a low-level architecture (LLA). The resulting design preserves the responsibility boundaries of the foundational framework while translating them into executable architectural structures, including 47 logical roles, versioned task graphs, capability-based agent selection, typed contracts, explicit runtime states, spatial validation mechanisms, governance controls, failure and recovery paths, and provenance records. The architecture is demonstrated through an end-to-end execution trace and analytically evaluated for requirements traceability, internal consistency, responsibility preservation, and technology independence. The resulting high-level-to-low-level design provides an implementation-facing bridge between the ANASSA framework and future system implementations, defining how governed spatial agentic workflows can be made inspectable, reconstructable, and testable without binding the architecture to a specific AI model, geospatial platform, communication protocol, or deployment environment.

title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
abstract: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open. science/r/scicuratebench-D885/.

title: RealityBench: Simulated Environments to Evaluate a Vision Language Model's Ability to Document Human Physical Work
abstract: Augmenting worker capabilities in the physical world through guidance has been a decades-long goal for AI agents. One key supporting capability is to understand what the worker is doing, seeing through the human's camera or smart glasses, and assist them in documentation. Despite advances in vision language models, their capabilities in these settings remain uncertain and are challenging to benchmark because most physical work data is proprietary, and involves too much variability to study in a principled manner. Unlike structured settings such as kitchens and warehouses that have predictable lighting, geometry, and objects, field-facing tasks such as rooftop solar installation and vehicle repair are unconstrained and high variance. Here, we model real-world physical work in Blender across eleven environments, incorporating variants in both image acceptability and documentation. The acceptability task asks whether a particular view would be suitable proof-of-work and documentation asks whether an agent can understand the task-relevant state of the environment from that view. Across 26 vision-language models, we find that top models largely solve documentation when the answer is text in frame, but are weak at reading measurements and at judging small parts and spatial relations, such as whether a tape measure leans. Acceptability is harder to pin down because human raters disagree with each other. Measured against a scorer that agrees with the raters' majority about as often as a single rater does, the best models cannot be distinguished from a single non-author rater, at a cost within the range of a human pass. In the three environments where we can trace acceptability errors, most wrong rejections come from misreading the scene rather than the requirement. On the three documentation questions for which we have real images, model rankings on rendered frames transfer to real images.

title: The Quantification of Replicability
abstract: What does it mean to measure the replicability of scientific results? Is it merely determining whether results are consistent across studies? Much of the existing literature on replicability draws conclusions exclusively from the comparison of study results, in terms of observed estimates, uses a variety of different metrics, and ultimately collapses the comparison into a binary verdict of success or failure. This fails to differentiate between repeated errors and corroboration of the shared generative effect. We develop a unified Bayesian framework in which distinct but related notions of replicability are formally defined and jointly embedded within a single inferential structure. A single model answers four complementary questions: agreement among independent studies; consistency between the individual studies and the shared generative effect; agreement between an existing body of evidence and a new study from the same super-population; inference on the shared generative effect. In practice, we suggest quantifying replicability through posterior probabilities relative to regions of practical relevance. We illustrate these ideas in an eQTL (expression quantitative trait locus) analysis assessing the replicability of a regulatory effect across human ancestral groups.

title: TheoPhysEval: Assessing AI agents at autonomous theoretical physics problem solving
abstract: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem. On average, agents show only small changes in accuracy when denied web search and access to background research papers, suggesting significant memorization of the literature. These results suggest that state-of-the-art agents can accurately perform concrete calculations required across theoretical physics research. We comment on the broader implications of these findings and discuss possible explanations for the current lack of agent-led breakthroughs in theoretical physics despite their outstanding problem-solving abilities.

title: Spatiotemporal Evolution and Associated Factors of Ecological Quality in the Poyang Lake Basin from 2000 to 2024 Based on Remote Sensing
abstract: Based on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform, this study constructed a Remote Sensing Ecological Index (RSEI) time series for the Poyang Lake Basin from 2000 to 2024. The analysis integrated Theil-Sen median trend estimation, the Mann-Kendall test, the Hurst exponent, and an interpretable machine-learning framework combining extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) to examine the spatiotemporal evolution of ecological quality and the factors associated with its spatial heterogeneity. The basin-average RSEI increased slightly from 0.693 in 2000 to 0.710 in 2024, indicating that the basin generally remained at a good ecological level, although interannual fluctuations were evident. Spatially, the RSEI showed a stable pattern of high values in the surrounding mountainous forest belts and lower values in the central plain, urbanized areas, and some lake and wetland zones. The ecological grade structure improved, with the proportion of areas classified as “excellent” increasing from 14.42% to 22.93%. Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall results showed that areas with historical ecological improvement were more extensive than areas of degradation. However, the Hurst exponent indicated that many pixels exhibited anti-persistent characteristics (H < 0.5), suggesting that future ecological trajectories may be uncertain rather than a simple continuation of historical improvement. XGBoost-SHAP analysis showed that land surface temperature (LST) and NDVI made the largest contributions to RSEI prediction. Because both variables are components of the RSEI, these results should be interpreted as index sensitivity to heat and vegetation conditions rather than independent causal effects. External variables, including GDP, population density, nighttime light intensity, elevation, and slope, showed additional predictive associations with spatial heterogeneity, conditional on the fitted model. These findings not only support differentiated watershed management but also provide a remote sensing perspective on long-term ecological quality changes associated with climate variability and human activities.

title: Reframing Authorship and Ethics in AI-driven and Immersive Architectural Environments: A Transdisciplinary Review
abstract: This article presents a comprehensive transdisciplinary review of the ways in which artificial intelligence(AI) and immersive technologies are transforming foundational concepts of authorship, ethics, and creativitywithin contemporary architecture and spatial design. The traditional notion of the architect as a singular,authoritative creator increasingly is challenged by computational processes that introduce generative, autonomous,and distributed forms of design agency. Through a synthesis of architectural theory, AI ethics, media studies,and posthuman philosophy, the review interrogates the shifting locus of authorship in design environmentsmediated by intelligent systems and extended reality (XR) platforms. At the core of this inquiry is an ontological reframing of authorship, informed by scholars such as RosiBraidotti, Tony Fry, Humberto Maturana, and Anne-Marie Willis. These frameworks position the architect notas an originator of form, but as a participant in a relational field of human and non-human agents, includingalgorithms, data, environments, and users. Adopting an ontological design lens, under which design practicesand their tools co‑produce forms of life and ways of world‑making, the article argues that AI/XR systems donot merely assist representation but actively configure professional authorship, agency, and ethics. This framinglinks practical workflows to normative guidance for disclosure, responsibility, and education. The review exploreshow generative design, neural networks, and parametric modeling redefine design intention and originality,situating authorship as a curatorial and computationally entangled process. In parallel, immersive media suchas virtual and augmented reality introduce new forms of user co-authorship and spatial manipulation, promptingethical questions about consent, agency, presence, and the authenticity of digital space. The article maps emerging discourses around design accountability, legal attribution, algorithmic bias, anddata governance, proposing an expanded ethical vocabulary for posthuman design practices. Through a criticalexamination of scholarly literature, experimental studios, and case-based applications, the review identifiesepistemological and practical challenges in reconciling human-centered traditions with distributed technologicalagency. Ultimately, this article argues for a redefinition of authorship as a dynamic, ethically situated, andontologically pluralistic concept in architecture. It advocates for the development of integrative frameworksthat embed ethical foresight and philosophical reflexivity into AI-augmented and immersive design methodologies.By repositioning the architect as a negotiator within hybrid systems of creativity and control, the articlecontributes a forward-looking perspective to architectural theory, technological practice, and planning discourse.
journal: Journal of Architectural/Planning Research and Studies (JARS)

title: Infinite Mindset and Self-Assessed Rice Farmer Capacity: Digital, Dynamic, and Managerial Pathways in West Aceh, Indonesia
abstract: Long-term orientations may support agricultural continuity, but their relationship with rice farmer capacity depends on more operational capabilities. This study examines digital capability, dynamic capability, and managerial competence as parallel statistical pathways linking infinite mindset to self-assessed rice farmer capacity in West Aceh, Indonesia. Descriptive analysis and independent partial least squares path modelling used the same 90 rice farmers, retaining 32 indicators and the direct mindset–capacity path. One missing capacity response was replaced by its observed indicator mean; an 89-case complete-response model provided a sensitivity check. Inference used 5,000 respondent-level bootstrap resamples, supplemented by location-cluster resampling and alternative specifications. Infinite mindset was positively associated with digital capability (β = 0.363), dynamic capability (β = 0.551), and managerial competence (β = 0.447). In the primary model, only managerial competence had a capacity association excluding zero (β = 0.560; 95% interval: 0.300–0.781). Its indirect association was 0.250 (0.122–0.418) and remained positive across the principal checks. Digital-path inference changed under location resampling, while the primary direct, digital-indirect, and dynamic-indirect intervals included zero. Capacity R² was 0.447, but restrictive-model residual diagnostics limited confirmatory interpretation. The findings support testing practical management routines alongside digital and adaptive support in rice extension, not established causal mediation or digital irrelevance.
journal: Best Journal of Administration and Management

title: A Comprehensive Review of Applications, Challenges, and Future Directions of Artificial Intelligence in Mortgage Lending
abstract: The mortgage lending industry is experiencing a significant transformation as it embraces Artificial Intelligence (AI) for its impact on decision-making, operations, risk management, and customer service. Many of the activities associated with mortgage processes can be automated and improved using technologies such as ML, DL, NLP, computer vision and generative AI, as these tasks are often document-driven, rule-based, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on manual work. Credit risk assessment, automated underwriting, fraud detection, intelligent document processing, property valuation, default prediction, mortgage servicing and customer support are just some of the ways AI is being applied to the credit industry. The study also identifies trends that are emerging such as explainable and agentic AI systems, which could help in making better mortgage decisions. But there are several challenges with the implementation of AI, including data privacy and security concerns, algorithmic bias, poor data quality, regulatory compliance, unreliable model performance amidst shifting market dynamics, and others. There are future developments anticipated in explainable and responsible AI, privacy-preserving learning, generative and multimodal AI, adaptive governance, and more human-AI collaboration. In summary, if implemented appropriately, AI can enhance mortgage lending processes by making them more efficient and intelligent, while ensuring transparency, fairness, security, and good governance.
journal: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology

title: Metal Powder Degassing Endpoint Detection With Remote Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy (RPOES)
abstract: Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIPing) is a critical manufacturing process that densifies metal powders or pre-formed components using simultaneous high temperature and pressure. A vital preparatory step involves the careful degassing of the powder and its containment canister to eliminate contaminants, which could otherwise compromise the integrity of the final product. This paper introduces Remote Plasma Optical Emission Spectroscopy (RPOES) as a robust solution for vacuum gas analysis during this phase. The RPOES instrument monitors residual gases—including water vapour, argon, and hydrogen—in real-time across a wide pressure range. Its remote sensing design eliminates the need for direct vacuum exposure, making it highly resistant to contamination. It enhances HIPing efficiency by significantly reducing processing time through precise endpoint detection, while also enabling leak checking and pump-down monitoring. Presented here are collaborative results from Gencoa and Synertech PM investigating the outgassing behaviour of metal powders prior to HIPing.

title: Assessment of Smallholder Farmers’ Knowledge, Adoption and Barriers to Agroecological Practices in the Western Highlands of Cameroon
abstract: Smallholder agriculture remains the backbone of rural livelihoods and food security in the Western Highlands of Cameroon. However, increasing climate variability, declining soil fertility, land degradation, and rising production costs continue to threaten agricultural productivity and household resilience. Agroecological practices have emerged as sustainable alternatives capable of improving soil health, conserving biodiversity, enhancing climate resilience, and reducing dependence on external agricultural inputs. Despite these recognized benefits, the adoption of agroecological practices by smallholder farmers remains uneven, largely due to socioeconomic, institutional, and technical constraints. This study assessed farmers' knowledge, adoption, perceived benefits, and barriers to the implementation of agroecological practices in the West Region of Cameroon. A cross-sectional survey involving 200 smallholder farmers was conducted using structured questionnaires administered through digital data collection platforms. Descriptive statistical analyses were employed to evaluate farmers' awareness, adoption rates, perceived benefits, and major constraints affecting implementation. The results revealed that approximately 72% of respondents were familiar with at least one agroecological practice. Mixed cropping (78%), organic soil fertilization (65%), and water conservation techniques (55%) were the most widely adopted practices. Farmers identified improved soil fertility (74%), enhanced resilience to climate variability (68%), improved soil moisture retention (64%), and reduced dependence on synthetic fertilizers (58%) as the principal benefits of agroecological farming. However, inadequate technical knowledge (68%), limited access to organic inputs (54%), financial constraints (47%), labour shortages (39%), and insufficient agricultural extension services (41%) significantly constrained wider adoption. The findings demonstrate that although agroecological practices are increasingly recognized by farming communities, substantial institutional and technical barriers continue to limit their large-scale adoption. Strengthening farmer training programmes, improving extension services, facilitating access to organic inputs, promoting farmer-to-farmer learning networks, and integrating renewable energy technologies such as biogas slurry into nutrient management systems could significantly accelerate the transition towards sustainable agricultural production in Cameroon. The study provides valuable evidence to guide policymakers, development partners, and agricultural extension agencies in designing interventions that promote resilient, climate-smart, and environmentally sustainable farming systems.
journal: Global Research in Environment and Sustainability

title: Comparative Evaluation of Deep Learning Architectures for Coastal Mean Sea Level
abstract: Accurate forecasting of mean sea level (MSL) is critical for coastal risk management, infrastructure planning, and climate adaptation, particularly along the low-lying Mid-Atlantic coast of the United States. This study presents a comprehensive comparative evaluation of four data-driven deep learning and neural network architectures, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and a lagged feed-forward neural network (FFNN), applied to seasonally adjusted monthly MSL records at the NOAA tide gauge station in Ocean City, Maryland (Station 8570283), spanning August 2002 through February 2025. All models share a standardized 24-month lookback window (lags 1–13 for the FFNN), 80/20 train/test split, Adam optimization, and early stopping, enabling controlled comparison. Models are evaluated using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and the coefficient of determination (R²) on held-out test data. Results indicate that the GRU achieves the best predictive performance among the neural architectures (RMSE = 0.0704 m, MAE = 0.0587 m, R² = 0.099), followed by the LSTM (RMSE = 0.0734 m, R² = 0.020). Even the GRU explained only about 10% of the test-period variance, and its RMSE was only about 3% lower than that of a persistence forecast. The CNN and FFNN both yield negative R² values (−0.219 and −0.907 respectively), which on this single test period placed the recurrent models ahead of the convolutional and feed-forward networks; this ranking was not stable across test periods (see below). A 24-month ensemble forecast is presented for all models through February 2027. The FFNN ensemble spread (±1σ across 20 independently initialized networks) is reported only as a measure of initialization variability; calibrated prediction intervals are derived from the ARIMA model and from rolling-origin forecast errors. When benchmarked under the identical protocol against persistence, seasonal-naïve, random walk with drift, linear trend, ARIMA, SARIMA and exponential smoothing (ETS) baselines, however, all three statistical time-series models outperformed every neural architecture: ARIMA(3,0,0) with a linear trend achieved the lowest test error (RMSE = 0.0642 m, R² = 0.250), and the GRU improved on a simple persistence forecast by only 3% in RMSE. These findings indicate that, for this univariate monthly record, the neural architectures tested did not add predictive value beyond well-specified linear time-series models; whether this holds at other stations has not yet been tested. An expandingwindow rolling-origin evaluation over 49 forecast origins (December 2012 – December 2024), with every model re-trained or re-estimated at each origin, confirmed this ranking at forecast horizons of 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 months: ARIMA had the lowest or near-lowest RMSE at every horizon (0.056–0.069 m), whereas the best neural model was 6–15% less accurate, and the single-split ranking of the neural architectures was not stable across test periods. All models predict the seasonally adjusted monthly MSL level in meters; training the networks on residuals from a training-period trend improved their accuracy and stabilised their forecasts but did not change their ranking relative to the statistical models. The NNAR model of R’s nnetar(), added as a separate benchmark, was far more accurate than the FFNN on the single split (RMSE = 0.0708 m) but was unstable at multi-step horizons and did not outperform ARIMA. Backtesting of the recursive multi-step forecasts showed that the neural models increasingly under-forecast with lead time, and that ARIMA prediction intervals were close to nominal coverage, whereas the FFNN ensemble spread and the simulated nnetar() intervals were far too narrow to serve as prediction intervals.

title: Probing Genomic Foundation Models with Splice-Variant Perturbations
abstract: As benchmarks saturate, traditional validation methods fail to capture the probabilistic representations of genomic foundation models. This study probes self-supervised generalists (NTv3 650M, Evo2 40B, Genos 10B) alongside task-specific specialists (SpliceAI, AlphaGenome, Borzoi) using a mechanistically focused paradigm centered on expert-curated single-nucleotide substitutions within the splicing regions of the exon-rich OPA1 gene. Extending this analysis across the broader corpus of OPA1 mutations, variants of uncertain significance (VUS), and an independent 65-gene dataset of spliceogenic mutations demonstrates that generalists can match task-specific networks. Training data scale, genetic diversity, and evolutionary context are key for capturing RNA splicing syntax, whereas sparse routing may constrain performance. Mechanistically, foundation models exhibit a compute-asymmetry: the Evo2 40B model frontloads compute into massive parameter scale to resolve single-nucleotide variants within a narrow 425-bp context window, whereas the bidirectional NTv3 650M model and the Genos 10B mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture backload compute to inference, requiring spatial logit aggregation and expansive context windows of up to 94 kb. Furthermore, classification accuracy across these foundation models benefitted from locus-specific thresholding rather than mutation-class calibration, exposing representation boundaries of the models.

title: Yoga Tourism and Local Economic Development in Uttarakhand: Assessment of Employment, Income, and Livelihood Opportunities
abstract: Uttarakhand is one of India's leading tourism states due to its Himalayan geographical location, natural beauty, spiritual traditions, religious sites, and rich heritage of Yoga and Ayurveda. Rishikesh, in particular, has gained international recognition as a major centre for yoga and meditation. In recent years, the concept of tourism has expanded beyond religious and traditional tourism to include health, yoga, spirituality, nature, and wellness tourism. This shift has created new opportunities for local economic development in Uttarakhand. Yoga tourism is not limited to yoga training or meditation; it is linked to various economic activities such as accommodation, food, transportation, local products, handicrafts, agriculture, Ayurveda, spa, training, guide services, and digital services. This research paper analyses the role of yoga tourism in Uttarakhand and its potential impact on local employment, income, and livelihoods. The study is primarily a descriptive and analytical inquiry based on secondary data, government policies, tourism statistics, and available literature. According to the Uttarakhand Tourism Department, a total of 59,550,277 tourists were recorded at the state's major tourist destinations in 2024, including 59,373,869 domestic and 176,408 foreign tourists. During the same period, 968,893 tourists were recorded in Rishikesh, including 4,857 foreign tourists. These statistics are crucial for understanding the economic potential of yoga and wellness tourism. The study concludes that yoga tourism in Uttarakhand can serve as a medium for direct and indirect job creation, local income generation, women's entrepreneurship, homestay development, demand for local agriculture and handicrafts, youth self-employment, and diversification of the rural economy. However, this requires local community-centric, eco-friendly, and skill-based tourism development. The State Tourism Policy 2023 emphasises developing yoga, meditation, and AYUSH traditions under health and wellness tourism, registering wellness service providers, improving quality, package creation, training, and skill development.
journal: International Journal of Recent Advances in Multidisciplinary Topics

title: AI-Powered Tools in English Language Education: Opportunities, Limitations, and Ethical Concerns
abstract: The increasing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into English language education has introduced significant changes in teaching methodologies, learner engagement, assessment practices, and the development of linguistic competencies. AI-powered tools, including intelligent tutoring systems, generative language models, automated writing evaluation platforms, adaptive learning applications, speech-recognition technologies, and conversational agents, are creating opportunities for personalized instruction, immediate feedback, autonomous learning, and interactive language practice. However, their educational benefits are accompanied by substantial limitations and ethical concerns involving algorithmic bias, inaccurate linguistic feedback, data privacy, academic dishonesty, digital inequality, cultural representation, and excessive technological dependence. This study critically examines the opportunities, limitations, and ethical implications of AI-powered tools in English language education through a qualitative, literature-based analytical approach. Drawing upon contemporary scholarship, including research published in the Stanzaleaf International Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies, the paper explores how technological assistance can support linguistic development without compromising creativity, critical thinking, learner independence, or the responsibilities of educators. The study proposes a Human-Centred Ethical AI Integration Framework that integrates pedagogical relevance, learner autonomy, teacher mediation, digital equity, and ethical accountability. The analysis suggests that AI-assisted English language education is most defensible when technological systems enhance rather than replace human interaction, contextual understanding, and independent language production. The paper concludes that the sustainable integration of AI requires comprehensive digital literacy, transparent institutional policies, professional development, and learner-centred pedagogical practices.
journal: Stanzaleaf International Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies

title: Ожидаемое влияние ИИ-агентов на организацию медицинской помощи: результаты социологического экспертного опроса
abstract: Аннотация. Статья посвящена проблематике, включающей оценку ожиданий медицинских работников в отношении влияния ИИ-агентов на организацию медицинской помощи и выявление межсекторных различий. В исследовании для сбора эмпирических данных использован метод анкетного опроса экспертов амбулаторно-стационарного звена государственных и частных медицинских организаций. В оценках использованы 10-балльные шкалы, агрегированные в домены эффективности, нагрузки, безопасности/доверия, экономики и ИТ-готовности. В результате исследования выявлено, что во всех доменах получены значения выше нейтрального уровня, а наивысшие — по безопасности пациентов. Выявлен высокий потенциал ИИ-агентов для оптимизации клинико-административных процессов. Проведенные расчеты продемонстрировали, что статистически значимых различий между секторами не имеется, но при этом сохраняется умеренный скепсис в отношении ИТ-готовности и передачи ИИ критически важных решений. Сделан вывод о том, что ИИ-агенты обладают значительным потенциалом трансформации системы здравоохранения, однако его реализация требует взвешенного подхода, сочетающего максимальное использование технологий с ответственным управлением присущими им рисками и неопределённостями. Annotation. The article is devoted to the problematics, including the assessment of expectations of medical workers regarding the impact of AI agents on the organization of medical care and the identification of intersectoral differences. In the study, the method of questionnaire survey of experts of the outpatient-inpatient link of public and private medical organizations was used to collect empirical data. In the assessments, 10-point scales were used, aggregated into domains of efficiency, load, safety/trust, economy and IT readiness. As a result of the study, it was revealed that in all domains, values above the neutral level were obtained, and the highest — on patient safety. The study identified a high potential for AI agents to optimize clinical and administrative processes. The calculations showed that there were no statistically significant differences between the sectors, but there was still moderate skepticism about the IT readiness and transfer of critical decisions to AI. The study concluded that AI agents have significant potential to transform the healthcare system, but their implementation requires a balanced approach that combines the maximum use of technology with responsible management of the inherent risks and uncertainties.
journal: Бюллетень Национального научно-исследовательского института общественного здоровья имени Н.А.Семашко

title: PRINCIPALS' MOTIVATIONAL STRATEGIES AND TEACHERS' JOB PERFORMANCE IN PUBLIC SECONDARY SCHOOLS IN KADUNA STATE, NIGERIA
abstract: This study investigated the relationship between principals' motivational strategies and teachers' job performance in public secondary schools in Kaduna State, Nigeria. Two objectives, two research questions and two null hypotheses guided the study, focusing on principals' recognition strategy and welfare strategy as predictors of teachers' job performance. The predictive correlational research design was adopted because it enables the researcher to establish not just association but the extent to which an independent variable forecasts a dependent variable. The population comprised 8,540 teachers drawn from 375 public secondary schools spread across the 23 Local Government Areas of Kaduna State. Using Taro Yamane's formula at a 5% margin of error, a sample of 382 teachers was drawn through a multi-stage sampling technique that combined stratification by senatorial zone with simple random and proportionate sampling. Data were collected using a researcher-designed instrument, the Principals' Motivational Strategies and Teachers' Job Performance Questionnaire (PMSTJPQ), whose construct validity was established by three experts in educational management and measurement and evaluation, and whose reliability, determined through Cronbach Alpha on a pilot sample, yielded coefficients of .81, .79 and .86 for the recognition, welfare and job performance sub-scales respectively, with an overall index of .84. Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions while simple linear regression was used to test the hypotheses at the .05 level of significance. Findings revealed that principals utilised recognition strategy (grand mean = 3.22) and welfare strategy (grand mean = 2.86) to a high extent, and that both recognition strategy (R² = .375, F(1,358) = 214.66, p < .05) and welfare strategy (R² = .237, F(1,358) = 111.14, p < .05) significantly predicted teachers' job performance. Both null hypotheses were rejected. The study concludes that principals' motivational strategies are strong predictors of teachers' job performance in Kaduna State and recommends deliberate policy attention to structured recognition schemes and improved welfare packages for teachers.
journal: International Journal of Library Science and Educational Research

title: General‐purpose agents in human‐machine teams: Can we preserve meaningful human control?
abstract: As General‐Purpose AI (GPAI) grows more capable of cross‐domain reasoning and multi‐agent coordination, it reshapes the design space of military human‐machine teams and introduces new opportunities for adaptability as well as new risks for Meaningful Human Control (MHC). The paper presents an integrated delegation framework for preserving MHC in GPAI‐enabled human‐machine teams. It combines play‐based task structuring, normative constraints, LLM‐mediated interaction, and an exploratory empirical evaluation with military professionals. Part of this framework is DIALOG, an LLM‐mediated interaction component that translates natural language into doctrine‐aligned plays, and builds up a context with ethical, legal, and operational constraints. We evaluate this framework in TNO's vehicle simulation facility, where five military professionals executed tactical missions using closed play, open play, and goal‐based delegation modes. Findings reveal a nuanced autonomy‐control trade‐off: operators initially favored higher‐autonomy modes but reverted to more structured control when confronted with unexpected or non‐doctrinal agent behaviors. The results highlight implications for MHC, transparency, and trust calibration, and point toward research directions for enhancing tactical competence, communication fidelity, and verifiability in GPAI‐enabled human‐machine teams.

title: Toward an enhanced scalability framework for human‐multi‐agent teams
abstract: As autonomous systems become increasingly capable, the deployment of Human‐Multi‐Agent Teams (HMATs) offers immense potential for executing complex, decentralized tasks. However, realizing this potential is constrained by a critical bottleneck: the cognitive and supervisory capacity of the human operator. While foundational fan‐out models established crucial groundwork for predicting this capacity, they are structurally limited to sequential, one‐to‐one interactions and rely on ambiguous variables that often produce overly optimistic predictions in real‐world environments. This article synthesizes a multi‐year empirical research program to present a comprehensive, new framework for modeling human‐autonomy scalability. First, we deconstruct the variables of legacy models into human and robot elements, demonstrating that true scalability is a relational property driven by human‐robot alignment rather than raw machine autonomy. We then validate the necessity of a mathematically bounded architecture to ensure predictive stability under operational uncertainty. Finally, we extend this framework to mathematically capture the paradigm shift toward group‐based, one‐to‐many teaming. By analyzing the results of a complex, multi‐agent simulation, we reveal the fundamental, quantifiable trade‐off between increasing team scale and maintaining human oversight, providing AI system designers with a validated blueprint for optimizing the next generation of human‐autonomy teams.

Is There a Human Premium in Negotiations? A Relational-Economic Tradeoff in Human vs. AI Bargaining
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs), increasingly enable AI to serve as an active counterpart in negotiation. Drawing on negotiation theory and mind perception research, this study examines whether attributed counterpart identity, that is, the belief that a negotiation counterpart is human rather than AI, influences relational evaluations, satisfaction, and outcomes in a mixed-motive bargaining context. In a randomized laboratory experiment, 205 participants negotiated apartment rent with the same LLM-based broker but were led to believe the counterpart was either human or AI. After correction across the five Hypothesis 1 comparisons, participants who believed they negotiated with a human reported higher perceived warmth and integrity; perceived competence was higher only in the unadjusted comparison. Participants in the Person condition also reported higher relational satisfaction and agreed to less favorable economic outcomes, paying higher final rents than those who believed they negotiated with AI. Exploratory analyses further suggested that attributed counterpart identity shaped how participants organized and described their post-negotiation experiences, with human-attributed counterparts eliciting more differentiated evaluations and more partnership-oriented descriptions. As AI becomes more common in negotiation, these results highlight the importance of accounting for the relational value people derive from believing they are negotiating with another person.

title: Improving field phenotyping accuracy in rice: a comparative study of smartphone image analysis and manual measurement
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract: Rice (Oryza sativa L.) production is threatened by bacterial leaf blight (BLB), particularly from the virulent K3a strain. Reliableand efficient phenotyping is essential for breeding resistant cultivars, but traditional manual methods are time-consuming and prone to subjectivity. This study assessed the accuracy of smartphone-based image analysis for measuring lesion length (LL) and lesion ratio (LR) in BLB-infectedrice. A total of 102 recombinant inbred lines (RILs) derived from Chamdongjin and Sindongjin were evaluated using both manual methods and imageanalysis. Images were captured in the field using a smartphone (12MP, 4000×3000 pixels), without any auxiliary equipment. The images were analyzedusing ImageJ and Python-based tools and compared with manual measurements. Image-based data showed strong correlation with manual results(r = 0.84–1.00), and principal component analysis (PCA) explained 94.14% of the variance, effectively distinguishing resistant and susceptible lines.Statistically significant differences were observed between groups (p < 0.01), confirming reliability. Images taken at 3x magnification showed highaccuracy (r = 0.88–0.92), while those at 1x magnification showed reduced accuracy (r = 0.76–0.79), likely due to the inclusion of surrounding plants—highlighting the importance of proper field design and image framing. This study suggests that smartphone-acquired images, even withoutauxiliary equipment, may serve as a feasible and sufficiently accurate source for image-based phenotyping. This accessible approach has the potential tosupport rapid, low-cost data collection in field settings, which could contribute to breeding and disease resistance research. Smartphone-based image measurements were strongly correlated with conventional measurements of rice bacterial leaf blight symptoms. Images captured at3×magnification showed stronger correlations with reference measurements than images captured at 1×magnification. Lesion ratio showed greaterconsistency across ImageJ and Python analyses than lesion length. Smartphone-based field imaging distinguished resistant and susceptible rice lineswithout additional imaging equipment.

title: Drivers and milk yield impacts of forage crop diversification in Napier grass-based smallholder dairy systems: evidence from Kenya
Contrasting sediment export despite similar hydrological responses in paired integrated crop-livestock watersheds
abstract: Runoff and sediment export are triggered by the same storms but need not scale proportionally across managed watersheds. We tested whether event-scale sediment export differed between two neighboring integrated crop-livestock watersheds after accounting for drainage area and the magnitude of runoff response under comparable rainfall forcing. Three years of 10-min hydrometric and turbidity monitoring were evaluated for 58 contemporaneous rainfall-runoff events in two neighboring subtropical grain-dairy headwater watersheds (0.67 and 1.14 km²). Event discharge volumes were converted to runoff depths before watershed comparison. Paired Wilcoxon tests, rank-based rainfall-response analyses, a direct runoff-sediment analysis, and sediment-discharge hysteresis were used to compare responses. Turbidity-derived suspended sediment concentrations were interpreted with explicit attention to calibration uncertainty at high concentrations. After normalization by drainage area, total runoff depth, baseflow depth, surface runoff depth, specific peak discharge, and runoff coefficient did not differ significantly between watersheds. In contrast, maximum suspended sediment concentration and specific sediment yield were markedly greater in the north watershed (p < 0.001), with maximum SSC reaching 25.6 g L− 1 versus 3.36 g L− 1. Surface runoff depth was strongly associated with specific sediment yield within both watersheds (Spearman rho = 0.81 and 0.79), but a pooled log-transformed model showed a strong watershed offset (p < 0.001), indicating substantially different sediment export at comparable runoff. Clockwise hysteresis predominated in both watersheds, whereas the hysteresis index did not differ significantly. The results support partial event-scale decoupling in the magnitude of runoff and sediment responses: hydrological response was broadly similar after area normalization, whereas sediment export differed strongly between watersheds. Because drainage area, riparian condition, livestock access, tillage, soil composition, and other attributes co-varied, these contrasts are interpreted as system-level associations rather than isolated causal effects. Management should therefore address both runoff-generation pathways and sediment-transfer connectivity.

title: Comparative impact of fuel exports, alternative and nuclear energy, and electricity consumption on economic growth: evidence from G20 economies
Integrating indigenous knowledge systems into regenerative agriculture for sustainable crop production in southern Africa
abstract: Agricultural production in Southern Africa is increasingly constrained by climate variability, declining soil fertility, water scarcity, biodiversity loss, and rising pest pressures, particularly within rain-fed smallholder farming systems. Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS), developed through generations of interaction between communities and local agroecosystems, offer context-specific approaches that align closely with the principles of regenerative agriculture. This review synthesizes evidence from 37 publications examining the contribution of IKS to sustainable crop production across Southern Africa. Particular attention is given to soil health, soil biological activity, water-use efficiency, ecological pest regulation, crop productivity, and climate resilience. The synthesis demonstrates that indigenous regenerative practices, including organic soil amendments, residue retention, crop diversification, intercropping, agroforestry, water harvesting, and botanical pest management, improve soil organic carbon, enhance microbial activity, increase water retention, and stabilize yields under climatic stress. Evidence further indicates that indigenous pest management strategies frequently maintain pest populations below economic injury thresholds, thereby reducing dependence on synthetic pesticides while supporting ecosystem services. The review highlights the convergence between IKS, agroecology, integrated pest management, conservation agriculture, and regenerative agriculture, and proposes pathways for integrating indigenous ecological indicators into decision-support systems, crop models, and precision agriculture technologies. Despite growing recognition of indigenous knowledge within sustainability and climate adaptation agendas, significant gaps remain in quantitative validation, longitudinal assessment, and integration into formal agricultural research and policy frameworks. The findings demonstrate that Indigenous Knowledge Systems constitute a scientifically credible and economically viable foundation for regenerative agriculture and contribute directly to Sustainable Development Goals 2 (Zero Hunger), 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), 13 (Climate Action), and 15 (Life on Land). Strengthening the integration of indigenous and scientific knowledge systems will be essential for building resilient, productive, and sustainable agricultural systems across Southern Africa and the broader Global South.

title: Accountability in smart contracts and agentic AI: How to address the responsibility gap and retain meaningful human control?
abstract: This conceptual paper examines the ethical challenges of ascribing responsibility when an Agentic AI embedded within a smart contract leads to harm or an unintended and undesirable outcome. It becomes exceedingly difficult in such scenarios to definitively assign moral or legal blame to any human actor (e.g., the programmer, deployer, or user). Applying the tripartite framework (attributability, answerability, and accountability) of responsibility and developing accountability as an institutional concept, we demonstrate how this challenge can be addressed. Separating attributability, answerability, and accountability yields an asymmetry that has gone unremarked. Accountability, being constituted by practices that can be designed in advance, with our four conditions under which such design is legitimate rather than arbitrary, emerges to be the sense where the gap can be closed. We also propose the visionary human-in-the-lead (HITL*) approach to related AI governance. Practical strategies such as implementing tailored smart contract regulations, and making accountability distributed across legal and organizational structures, offer an actionable path to bridge the responsibility gap and maintain meaningful human control in the governance of smart contracts and Agentic AI.

title: Smart agriculture improves nitrogen use efficiency yield prediction and sustainability in dryland mixed crop livestock systems
publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
abstract: Mixed crop-livestock systems in dryland regions play a critical role in ensuring food security in the Global South; however, they are confronted with several challenges, including unpredictable rainfall patterns, nutrient depletion, and low productivity levels. The integration of advanced agricultural technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and remote sensing, presents transformative opportunities for enhancing the efficacy of these systems. This paper investigates how intelligent agricultural tools can improve nitrogen management, boost productivity in both crops and livestock, and promote overall farm sustainability. Strategies such as intercropping alfalfa with corn silage, utilizing remote sensing for real-time monitoring, and implementing precision fertilization techniques directly address fundamental issues such as nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), soil health, and feed quality. Additionally, the application of intelligent yield estimation models and nutrient recovery methods further optimizes resource utilization. The integration of machine learning algorithms with satellite data enhances the accuracy of yield predictions, thereby facilitating informed decision-making and bolstering economic resilience. Despite these promising advancements, various barriers including limited digital accessibility, data deficiencies, and socio-economic constraints impede the widespread adoption of these technologies. Therefore, it is essential to implement policy support, develop necessary infrastructure, and promote farmer-centered co-innovation to scale these solutions effectively. This study concludes that the incorporation of smart agriculture within integrated crop-livestock systems can significantly enhance sustainability, productivity, and resilience in dryland regions. The integration of smart agricultural tools significantly enhances nitrogen use efficiency and overall productivity in crop-livestock systems. The practices of intercropping and intelligent monitoring contribute to improved sustainability and favorable economic outcomes. Addressing data gaps and overcoming digital barriers are critical factors for the widespread adoption of advanced agricultural technologies. The integration of smart agricultural tools significantly enhances nitrogen use efficiency and overall productivity in crop-livestock systems. The practices of intercropping and intelligent monitoring contribute to improved sustainability and favorable economic outcomes. Addressing data gaps and overcoming digital barriers are critical factors for the widespread adoption of advanced agricultural technologies.

title: Molecular and environmental regulation of floral development, flowering, and sex differentiation in angiosperms
abstract: Floral organ development and sex differentiation are key processes controlling plant reproduction and yield in angiosperms. The ABCDE model explains floral organ identity through the combinatorial action of MADS-box transcription factors; however, additional regulators such as SPL, WOX, NAC, TGA, and AGL6 further refine organ specification and meristem activity. Flowering is regulated by environmental signals, including photoperiod, temperature, and vernalization, as well as endogenous pathways involving hormones, sugars, and age-related microRNAs. Central regulatory modules, such as CO–FT, FLC, and miR156–miR172, integrate these signals to control the transition to flowering. Hormonal crosstalk and metabolic cues, particularly carbon–nitrogen balance, further modulate gene expression and developmental outcomes. Sex differentiation adds another layer of complexity to floral development. Although hermaphroditism is predominant among angiosperms, monoecious and dioecious species produce unisexual flowers through diverse genetic, developmental, hormonal, and environmental mechanisms, with sex-linked loci and differentiated sex chromosomes contributing in some lineages. These mechanisms contribute to reproductive diversity and adaptation in angiosperms. This review summarizes recent advances in the molecular and environmental regulation of floral development, flowering, and sex differentiation, highlighting gene regulatory networks, transcriptional control, and environmental signals, with implications for future research and crop improvement.

title: Comparative assessment of machine learning algorithms and Ordinary Kriging for predictive mapping of soil clay content in a tropical Guinea Savanna
abstract: Clay content is an important determinant of soil physical and chemical behaviour, influencing water retention, nutrient availability, and agricultural productivity. Accurate spatial prediction of clay distribution is therefore important for digital soil mapping and sustainable land management. This study compared Random Forest (RF), Cubist, Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), and Ordinary Kriging (OK) for predictive mapping of clay content in the tropical Guinea Savanna of Kaduna State, Nigeria. Legacy soil profile data collected between 2005 and 2024 (n = 156) were integrated with terrain, climatic, and Sentinel-2-derived environmental covariates generated in Google Earth Engine. Model performance was evaluated using R2, root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and computational time, while SHAP analysis was used to assess predictor importance. Clay content varied substantially (2.3–71.0%), with the ML models predicting higher values mainly along drainage corridors and lower landscape positions. Mean annual precipitation, elevation, Topographic Position Index, EVI, and slope showed the highest mean SHAP importance, although their relative contributions varied among models. Cubist achieved the highest validation accuracy (R2 = 0.67, RMSE = 8.32%, MAE = 6.37%) and shortest execution time (0.14 s), followed by RF (R2 = 0.56) and GBM (R2 = 0.45), while OK recorded R2 = 0.08 and RMSE = 12.44%. Under the configurations tested, environmental-covariate-driven ML models provided more accurate predictions than OK. Cubist was the best-performing model among the evaluated configurations, demonstrating the potential of ML-based digital soil mapping for clay characterization and soil resource management in data-scarce tropical environments.

CXCL16-driven neutrophil extracellular traps promote osteoporosis in APP/PS1 mice by disrupting bone remodeling.
abstract: Patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) often exhibit abnormal bone loss alongside cognitive impairment. However, the mechanisms linking these two conditions remain insufficiently understood. We first employed amyloid precursor protein/presenilin 1 (APP/PS1) mice as the experimental model and demonstrated that they exhibit significant bone loss concurrent with cognitive impairment. Subsequently, we analyzed public datasets for AD and osteoporosis (OP) and identified CXC chemokine ligand 16 (CXCL16) as a shared hub gene between the two diseases. Transcriptomic sequencing further showed increased CXCL16 expression in the femoral tissue of APP/PS1 mice. Immunoblot analysis of brain and bone tissues, together with serum enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), verified the systemic elevation of CXCL16. These findings suggest that CXCL16 may link cognitive impairment with bone loss in APP/PS1 mice. In vitro experiments showed that CXCL16 did not directly affect the differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells or bone marrow-derived macrophages. Instead, CXCL16 acted through neutrophils by promoting their migration and potentiating PMA-stimulated neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. Conditioned medium from NET-producing neutrophils inhibited osteogenic differentiation and promoted osteoclastogenesis. In APP/PS1 mice, antagonism of CXCR6, the cognate receptor for CXCL16, with ML339 improved trabecular bone microarchitecture and osteogenic activity and alleviated cognitive impairment. Degradation of NETs with deoxyribonuclease I (DNase I) produced similar effects. Collectively, these results implicate CXCL16-associated enhancement of NET formation in AD-related skeletal deterioration and highlight the CXCL16-NETs pathway as a possible intervention target for maintaining bone homeostasis.
